passages.title: The pleading woman and the zihār ruling
passages.tafsir:
A woman came to the Prophet ﷺ with a marriage problem for which no ruling had yet been revealed, argued her case, and directed her complaint to Allah — and the opening of a whole sūrah came down about her. Ayah 1 tells us her complaint was heard; ayat 2–4 dismantle a cruel pre-Islamic custom called **ẓihār** and replace it with a graded, merciful expiation.

## The woman whose complaint reached the seventh heaven

Her name was Khawlah bint Thaʿlabah — also transmitted as Khuwaylah, and as Khawlah bint Mālik ibn Thaʿlabah; Ibn Kathīr notes these are all close to one another and Allah knows best. Her husband was Aws ibn aṣ-Ṣāmit.

Imam Ahmad recorded her own account. She began: "By Allah! Allah sent down the beginning of Sūrat al-Mujādilah in connection with me and Aws ibn aṣ-Ṣāmit." Aws had grown old and difficult. One day she argued with him about something and he said, out of anger, "You are like my mother's back to me." He went out and sat with some of his people, then came back wanting to be intimate with her. She refused: "No, by the One in Whose Hand is the soul of Khuwaylah! You will not have your way with me after you said what you said, until Allah and His Messenger issue judgement about our case." When he pressed her regardless, she pushed him away — he was an old man. She then went to one of her neighbours, borrowed a garment from her, and went to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, she went to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ *seeking redress for her problem according to the Sharīʿah*.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in what happened next. Up to that point the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had received no revelation concerning that legal issue, so he told her plainly, "I have not yet received any ordinance regarding your matter," and gave his own opinion according to the common custom people knew: "In my opinion, you have become forbidden to him." That is when she pleaded:

> "O Allah's Messenger! He spent my wealth, exhausted my youth and my womb bore abundantly for him. When I became old, unable to bear children, he pronounced the ẓihār formula on me. Where shall I go and how will my children do their living?"

In another version she argued the law itself: "My husband did not mention the word 'divorce', so how can this be counted as divorce?" In another she pleaded to Allah: "O Allah! I direct my complaint to You." Qurṭubī, cited in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, records that when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ pleaded his inability to do anything for her, she uttered spontaneously: *you receive ordinances in all matters — then how is it that no ordinance was revealed to you in my case?* And the verse was revealed: **"…and complains to Allah."**

In the narration Imam Ahmad recorded, the Prophet ﷺ also said to her, "O Khuwaylah! Your cousin is an old man, so have taqwā of Allah regarding him." Then, she says, "Before I departed, parts of the Qur'an were revealed about me." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ felt the hardship upon receiving the revelation as he usually did, then became relieved, and said: "O Khuwaylah! Allah has revealed something about you and your spouse" — and he recited to her from *"Indeed Allah has heard…"* through to *"…and for disbelievers there is a painful torment."*

**How ʿĀʼishah heard it.** Imam Ahmad recorded that she said: "All praise be to Allah, Who hears all voices." The woman who disputed came to the Prophet ﷺ and argued with him while ʿĀʼishah was in another part of the room, unable to hear what she said — and Allah revealed this ayah. In the narration Ibn Abī Ḥātim collected she said: "Blessed is He, Whose hearing has encompassed all things. I heard what Khawlah bint Thaʿlabah said while some of it I could not hear." Al-Bukhārī collected this ḥadīth without a chain of narration in the Book of Tawḥīd in his Ṣaḥīḥ; an-Nasāʼī, Ibn Mājah, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Ibn Jarīr also collected it. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān transmits her words in a similar form — *"despite being so close to her in the same room."* Human hearing failed across a single room. Allah's hearing did not.

**And ʿUmar's response to her.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates from Ibn Kathīr that ʿUmar al-Fārūq, once on his way with some of the blessed Companions, came across a woman who stopped him. He instantly stopped and listened attentively to her with his head bent down, and did not move until she had completed what she wanted to say. Some of them said, "O Commander of the Faithful! You have held back such a large group of people for such a long time on account of this old lady!" He answered: "Do you know who this lady is? She is Khawlah — the lady whose complaint was heard in the seventh heaven. So how can ʿUmar not listen to her? She should be heard for a longer period of time and with greater attention. By Allah! If she did not take leave of her own accord, I would have stood with her here till nightfall."

## "Allah has heard" — and the close of ayah 1

The sūrah opens with **qad samiʿa Allāh** — *Indeed Allah has heard*. Before any ruling is issued, the first thing revealed is that her voice registered with her Lord. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the point directly: these verses do not only lay down the rule of the Sharīʿah pertaining to ẓihār and redress the grievances of women placed in such an awkward situation — the first verse is also *in honour of the pleading lady*, consoling her, in that it says that Allah was listening to her words while she was pleading her case.

The word behind "who disputes with you" is from **mujādalah**, which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān defines as "to plead, argue or dispute consistently and convincingly about one's problem or case." And **tashtakī ilā Allāh**: she takes her complaint *to Allah* — in her own words as Imam Ahmad recorded them, "until Allah and His Messenger issue judgement about our case."

Ayah 1 then closes: *"And Allah hears the argument between you both. Verily, Allah is All-Hearer (Samīʿ), All-Seer (Baṣīr)."* ʿĀʼishah's own reaction is the believing response to such names: not speculation, but awe — "Blessed is He, Whose hearing has encompassed all things."

## What ẓihār was, and why the Qur'an calls it a lie

Ibn Kathīr explains that *ẓihār* is derived from **az-Zahr**, meaning "the back." During the time of Jāhiliyyah, when a man wanted to declare ẓihār towards his wife, he would say, "To me, you are like the back of my mother." Qurṭubī, cited in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, notes that the word *zahr* ("back") here refers metonymically to the stomach or womb.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the Sharīʿah definition precisely. Certain women are permanently forbidden to a man — his mother, sister, daughter and others in the prohibited degree — and although looking at such women is permissible in general, looking at some parts of their body (the abdomen, the back and so on) is not. Ẓihār is *to compare one's wife with any such part of the body of such a prohibited woman*.

That was one of the ways they issued divorce in that era — but worse than divorce. In the case of divorce, it was possible to retract and take the wife back. In the case of ẓihār, according to the old Arab custom, all conjugal relations ceased permanently: she became permanently and absolutely forbidden, with no possibility of restoring the marriage. That is the trap Khawlah was in: an old woman, her wealth spent, her children to feed, and no legal door out.

Ayah 2 shatters the premise: **"…they cannot be their mothers. None can be their mothers except those who gave them birth."** Ibn Kathīr: when the husband says to his wife that she is like his mother, or like the back of his mother, *she does not become his mother* — rather his mother is she who gave birth to him. Words do not remake reality. Hence the verdict on the utterance itself: **"they utter an ill word and a lie"** — which Ibn Kathīr glosses as "false and sinful speech." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out both halves: calling one's wife one's mother is *contrary to truth and fact*, and it is *a heinous sin*.

**Two reforms in these verses**, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets them out. First, ẓihār has been declared a sinful act. If a man needs to separate from his wife, he must choose the method of divorce; ẓihār should not be resorted to, because the utterance is absurd and false. Second, if an ignorant person, or one unacquainted with the legal formalities of Islam, does utter the formula, his wife does not become permanently unlawful to him — nor does he have an open licence to do as he wishes. He cannot take back his wife without first paying the prescribed expiation. Ibn Kathīr states the mercy plainly: Allah allowed this Ummah to pay expiation for this statement and did not render it as a divorce, contrary to the case during the time of Jāhiliyyah.

At the end of ayah 2 the door opens: **"And verily, Allah is Oft-Pardoning, Oft-Forgiving."** Ibn Kathīr explains what is being pardoned — "what you used to do during the time of Jāhiliyyah, and what accidentally slips out of your mouth, unintentionally." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads it as an invitation: Allah in His great mercy has made allowance for man's weaknesses and is always ready to forgive his lapses, *provided he comes to Allah with a penitent heart and makes amends*. Note what Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds: the penalty is imposed for the purpose of making the wife lawful again — ẓihār in itself is not the cause of the expiation. Ẓihār is a heinous sin for which repentance and seeking pardon and forgiveness is absolutely necessary in its own right.

## "Then go back on what they said" — where the scholars differ

Ayah 3 makes the expiation conditional: *"And those who make unlawful to them their wives by ẓihār and wish to free themselves from what they uttered…"* What exactly is this "going back"? Ibn Kathīr reports genuine differences among the imams:

- **Ash-Shāfiʿī**: "It means to keep her for a while after the ẓihār, without divorcing her, even though he is able to do so."
- **Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal**: "To return to having sexual relations with her or to merely intend to do so, but only after he pays the expiation mentioned in the ayah for his statement."
- **Mālik** (as quoted from him): it is the intention to have sexual relations, or to keep her, or actually having sexual intercourse.
- **Saʿīd ibn Jubayr**: if they want to return to the sexual intercourse which was forbidden between them.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds, from Ibn ʿAbbās (via Mazharī), that "retract" carries the sense of *regret*: they regret what they said and wish to be intimate with their wives again. It also notes a grammatical point — the preposition *lām* in *yaʿūdūna li-mā qālū* is used in the sense of *ʿan*, "from": going back *on* what they said.

**"Before they touch each other."** ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that "touching" here refers to sexual intercourse; similar was said by ʿAṭāʼ, az-Zuhrī, Qatādah and Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān. Az-Zuhrī added, "He is not to kiss or touch her until he pays the expiation." Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī held the prohibition to be intercourse itself, and did not see any harm in doing what is less than that before the expiation is paid.

The Sunan compilers recorded from ʿIkrimah, from Ibn ʿAbbās, that a man said, "O Allah's Messenger! I pronounced ẓihār on my wife, but then had sexual intercourse with her before I paid the expiation." The Messenger ﷺ said, "May Allah grant you His mercy — what made you do that?" He said, "I saw the adornment she was wearing shining in the moon's light." The Prophet ﷺ said, "Then do not touch her until you do what Allah, the Exalted and Most Honoured, has ordered you to do." At-Tirmidhī said, "Ḥasan Gharīb Ṣaḥīḥ"; Abū Dāwūd and an-Nasāʼī also recorded it. Note the tone: a duʿā for mercy and a gentle question before the correction — and the penalty is not waived by the slip.

## The three steps of expiation

Ayah 3 gives the first step, ayah 4 the remaining two, in strict order:

1. **Freeing a slave**, before the couple touch each other. Ibn Kathīr notes a subtle ease here: this ayah mentions any slave, not only believing servants as in the case of the expiation for unintentional killing.
2. **If he finds none — fasting two successive months**, again before they touch each other.
3. **If he is unable to do so — feeding sixty of the poor.**

Ibn Kathīr notes that this ordering is explained by the ḥadīths that prescribe these penalties in this order, just as in the ḥadīth collected in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs about the man who had sexual intercourse with his wife during the day in Ramadan.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives practical measures for the third option: the expiation is fulfilled if one poor person is given two meals for sixty days, or by giving two meals to sixty poor persons on a single day — in each case the poor should be fed to their fill — or else by giving a poor person about 1.6 kg of wheat, or 2.12 kg of dates or barley, for sixty days, or the equivalent price. The fuller details are set out in the texts of Islamic jurisprudence.

**And it was applied with exactly this gentleness.** In the narration Imam Ahmad recorded, the Prophet ﷺ told Khuwaylah: "Command him to free a slave." She said he did not have any to free. "Let him fast for two consecutive months." She said, "By Allah! He is an old man and cannot fast." "Let him feed sixty poor people a *wasq* of dates." She said he had nothing of that either. He ﷺ said, "We will help him with a basket of dates" — and she said, "And I, O Allah's Messenger! I will help him with another." He said: "You have done a righteously good thing. So go and give away the dates on his behalf, and take care of your cousin." She said, "I did that." Abū Dāwūd also collected this ḥadīth in the Book of Divorce in his Sunan.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates a separate account from Ibn Kathīr — recorded, it says, in the Traditions — in which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ called for the husband, and noticed that he was a weak-sighted old man. He recited to him the verses resolving his case and worked down the same three options. The man could not free a slave; and of fasting he said, "By Him Who has sent you as the true Messenger, if I do not have two or three meals a day, I lose my sight completely." Told to feed sixty poor people, he said he had no ability for that either unless he was helped. So the Prophet ﷺ gave him some food grain, and other people gathered more for him until it amounted to the measure of *ṣadaqat al-fiṭr* for sixty poor men, and in this way the expiation was made.

Two tellings, one shape: the law is enforced, the marriage is repaired, and nobody is crushed.

## "So that you may believe" — the close of ayah 4

*"That is in order that you may have perfect faith in Allah and His Messenger."* Ibn Kathīr: 'We legislated this so that you acquire this trait.' Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that "belief" here implies *acting upon* the sacred laws and ordinances, obeying the commandments of Allah and His Messenger — faith proven in compliance, not merely professed.

*"These are the limits set by Allah"* — Ibn Kathīr: the things He has forbidden, so do not transgress them. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads the phrase as saying that the laws of expiation are limits set by Allah which it is prohibited to exceed, and that in matters of marriage, divorce, ẓihār and the like, Islam has abolished all traces of the pre-Islamic pagan customs and set down a just and approved code in their place. The final warning, *"and for disbelievers there is a painful torment,"* means, as Ibn Kathīr puts it, that those who do not believe and do not abide by the rulings of Islamic legislation should never think they will be saved from the torment; rather theirs will be a painful torment in this life and the Hereafter.

## Living it

**Never weaponise words in a marriage.** The whole passage begins with a man saying something out of anger. Words spoken in a moment of temper carried consequences that required freeing a slave, or two months of fasting, to undo. If a separation is genuinely needed, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is blunt: he must choose the method of divorce, and not resort to a formula that is absurd and false.

**A woman's rights are not left dangling.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān addresses the case where a man commits ẓihār and does not wish to take his wife back: the expiation is then not obligatory on him — but destroying a wife's conjugal rights is unlawful. If she demands, he must either pay the expiation and take her back, or divorce her and set her free from the bond of marriage. If he does neither, she has the right to apply to a qāḍī or an Islamic court to compel him, so that she may contract a second marriage. Khawlah's instinct — to seek a ruling rather than simply endure — is embedded in the law itself.

**Take your complaint upward.** She complained to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and she complained to Allah: "O Allah! I direct my complaint to You." The answer came down, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that Allah not only made matters easy for her — the rule has been eternally enshrined in the Holy Qur'an for all sensible people to follow.

**And listen the way ʿUmar listened.** A leader with a crowd behind him stopped and bent his head for an old woman, because he knew whose complaint Allah had heard. If the Lord of the worlds heard what ʿĀʼishah could not catch from across the same room, no believer is too busy to hear someone out.

passages.title: Those who defy Allah will be debased
passages.tafsir:
These two ayat answer a simple question: what actually happens to someone who sets himself against Allah and His Messenger ﷺ? The answer comes in two movements — disgrace for those who oppose (ayah 5), and then, on the Day of Resurrection, a full and detailed telling of everything they did (ayah 6). What holds the passage together is a single thread: **the defiant think their opposition succeeds and their deeds disappear. Both assumptions are false.**

## Where this comes from in the surah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the link explicit. In the preceding verse, stress was laid on keeping to the Divine limits and to the sacred laws of Islam. The current verse warns those who oppose or reject them. So this is not an abstract threat dropped into the surah — it is the consequence attached to the boundary that was just drawn. Where there is a limit, there is a verdict for those who trample it.

## "Those who defy Allah and His Messenger"

Ibn Kathir's gloss on the phrase is worth pausing over. He explains it as those who defy Allah and His Messenger ﷺ **and contradict His commandments**. That is the shape of the offence being described. It is not doubt, not weakness, not the sin of a person who knows he has slipped. It is a posture — taking a stand on the other side of the line, setting your will against His.

Notice too that Allah and His Messenger ﷺ are named together in the ayah. The opposition being described is a single act aimed at both.

## "Will be debased" — *kubitū*

Ibn Kathir unpacks the key word with three terms: they will be **humiliated, cursed and disgraced**.

And the humiliation is the point. Look at how ayah 5 ends: **"And for the disbelievers is a disgraceful torment."** Ibn Kathir explains that this is "as just recompense for their arrogant refusal to follow, obey and submit to the religion of Allah." The punishment is fitted to the crime with precision. The sin was arrogance — refusing to lower oneself before Allah. So the punishment is not simply pain; it is *disgrace*. The one who would not be humbled willingly is humbled unwillingly. Pride is answered with degradation, exactly and deliberately.

## "Just as those before them were debased"

The ayah does not stop at the verdict — it points backwards. Ibn Kathir: they will be humiliated, cursed and disgraced "just as what happened to their like were before them."

That phrase, *their like*, carries the weight. The people being warned are not the first of their kind; earlier generations took the same position and met the same disgrace.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out both halves of what awaits: **"Their profane designs shall be foiled and they shall be humiliated in this world and a condign torment shall be inflicted on them in the Hereafter."** (*Condign* is an older English word for a punishment exactly matched to what was earned.)

That is a striking claim, and it deserves to be heard clearly. The one who fights Allah's religion imagines he is building something. Maʿārif says the plan itself will be foiled — and that the humiliation is not postponed entirely to the next life. Part of it falls in this world.

## "And We have sent down clear Ayat"

Between the verdict and the torment, ayah 5 inserts something that looks like a change of subject but is actually the argument: **"And We have sent down clear Ayat."**

Ibn Kathir's comment is short and devastating in what it implies: this means that "none contradicts or opposes them, except a disbeliever, rebellious, sinner."

In other words, the signs are *clear*. Their clarity is what removes any excuse. If the evidence were murky, opposition could be honest confusion. But when the ayat have been sent down plain, opposing them stops being an intellectual position and becomes a moral one. The word Ibn Kathir uses — *contradicts* — is telling: the person is not failing to understand the sign, he is setting himself against it. This is why the humiliation in this passage reads as just, and not merely as power crushing weakness. Allah made the truth clear before He judged anyone for turning from it.

## Ayah 6: the Day everything is handed back

Ayah 6 moves the scene: **"On the Day Allah resurrects them all together, He will then inform them of what they did."**

Ibn Kathir explains "all together" as referring to the Day of Resurrection, when Allah **will gather the early and the latter generations in one area**. Every generation that ever lived, in a single place. Nothing is left behind in the past; the past is brought forward and assembled.

Then comes the confrontation — and note that it is described as *information*. "He will inform them of what they did." Ibn Kathir: "He will tell them all that they did **in detail, whether good or evil**." Two things stand out. First, the level of resolution — detail, not summary. Second, that this telling includes the good as well as the evil; nothing is dropped from the record in either direction.

## "Allah has kept account of it, while they have forgotten it"

This is the heart of ayah 6, and both commentaries pause on it.

Ibn Kathir: it means "Allah recorded and kept all these actions, even though they have forgotten what they did."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the forgetting, and the explanation lands uncomfortably close to home. A person is unable to remember and recall his transgressions **because he treats them as trivial and insignificant**. The forgetting is not innocent. It is the aftermath of a habit of not taking wrongs seriously. Whatever you file as "nothing" is what your memory will not bother to keep.

But — and this is the sentence's whole force — **the record was never yours to keep.** Maʿārif continues: they are all recorded and kept safely with Allah, even though the humans have done the actions and forgotten them; and Allah will call them to give an account of them on the Day of Resurrection and chastise them.

So the deed and the memory of the deed part company. The deed goes into a preserved account; the memory evaporates. On that Day the two are reunited, and the shock of ayah 6 is not that a person is punished for something he denies — it is that he is *told*, in detail, about something he no longer remembered doing. He forgot; Allah did not.

## "And Allah is Witness over all things"

Ayah 6 closes by naming the ground of all of this. Ibn Kathir explains the phrase to mean: **nothing escapes His knowledge, and no matter is hidden from Him or escapes His complete observation.**

Sit with that as it stands. Human witnessing is partial — we see a slice, we misremember, we are absent for most of what happens. Nothing at all escapes His knowledge or His observation. The threat of ayah 5 and the reckoning of ayah 6 rest entirely on this: the One who judges missed nothing.

## Living it

**Take the small things seriously.** The most practical line in this passage belongs to Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: a person cannot recall his transgressions because he treats them as trivial and insignificant. If that is the mechanism of forgetting, then the remedy is the reverse — refuse to file anything as insignificant. The sin you would be embarrassed to have read back to you in detail is the sin to repent from now, while you still remember it exists.

**Do not measure opposition to Allah's religion by how strong it looks.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the designs of those who oppose Allah and His Messenger ﷺ shall be foiled, that they shall be humiliated in this world, and that a condign torment awaits them in the Hereafter. A believer watching that opposition from the outside is not watching a contest with an uncertain result.

**Let the clarity of the ayat land on you before it lands on anyone else.** Ibn Kathir says none contradicts or opposes clear signs except a disbeliever, a rebel, a sinner. That is a mirror before it is a verdict on others: where in my own life do I know exactly what Allah has said and continue to live around it?

**And take comfort in the same attribute that terrifies.** "Allah has kept account of it" is a threat to the defiant — but Ibn Kathir notes that Allah will tell them all that they did "in detail, whether good or evil." The same perfect record that loses no sin loses no act of obedience either. The prayer no one saw, the patience no one thanked you for, the wrong you swallowed for the sake of Allah — you may forget it. He has kept the account.

passages.title: No secret counsel without Allah present
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat are about **whispering** — the huddled, private conversation that leaves the person walking past it feeling watched and afraid. The passage answers that fear at the deepest possible level: there is no such thing as a closed meeting. Allah is present at every one of them by His knowledge. Ayah 7 establishes that truth about Allah; ayah 8 exposes a group in Madinah who whispered anyway; ayah 9 turns to the believers and tells them what their own private talk must be for; ayah 10 names the real author of anxious whispering — Shayṭān — and tells the believer where to put his heart instead.

## The scene in Madinah

Ibn Kathir reports from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, that the people described in ayah 8 as "those who were forbidden to hold secret counsels" were the Jews — and Muqatil bin Hayyan said the same, filling in the picture: the Prophet ﷺ had a peace treaty with the Jews of Madinah. When one of the Prophet's Companions would pass by a gathering of theirs, they would start speaking among themselves in secret, so that the believer walking by would think they were plotting to kill or harm him. Muqatil adds a detail you can feel: the man would become afraid for his safety and **change the route he was taking**. The Prophet ﷺ told them to stop these whispering sessions. They did not listen, and carried on. Then this ayah came down about them.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the same account among the several occasions of revelation for this sūrah's middle section, noting that they would confer "in such a manner as to arouse suspicion and anxiety in the mind of the believer." It also records that the hypocrites of Madinah held their own secret conferences, and that ayah 9 and ayah 10 came down in connection with that.

So this is not an abstract discussion of privacy. It is about intimidation by body language — a weapon that costs nothing, leaves no evidence, and works entirely on the imagination of the victim.

## Ayah 7: the meeting with an uninvited Witness

Ayah 7 opens with **a-lam tara** — "Have you not seen?" — a question that does not want an answer, only your attention. What follows, in Ibn Kathir's words, is Allah "informing of His knowledge encompassing all creation, observing it, hearing their speech and seeing them, wherever they may be and in whatever condition they may be in."

The key word of the whole passage arrives here: **najwā**. Ibn Kathir glosses "there is no najwā of three" as *secret consultation* of three — not idle chat but a huddle with a purpose. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains why such huddles feel so secure to the people inside them: "Secret conferences are normally convened with special confidants to whom secrets are imparted trustingly. Members of the secret society are satisfied that they will not be betrayed. It is on the basis of this confidence that evil people design plots to oppress someone, or to kill him, or to usurp his wealth and property." The whole enterprise runs on one assumption — *nobody else is hearing this*. Ayah 7 demolishes that assumption in a single line.

**"He is their fourth… He is their sixth."** Notice the shape of the sentence. Allah does not say "He knows about them." He says He is *with* them, counted into the gathering: three, and He is the fourth; five, and He is the sixth. Then the ayah closes every loophole before anyone can look for one — "nor of less than that or more but He is with them wheresoever they may be." Fewer, more, anywhere: there is no configuration of a secret meeting that excludes Him.

**What "with them" means.** Ibn Kathir reports that several scholars mentioned there is a consensus that this "with" refers to Allah's **knowledge** — He is watching them and perfectly hearing their speech, whether uttered aloud or in secret. Ibn Kathir affirms this and adds that the meaning is only strengthened when we hold alongside it the certainty that His hearing encompasses all things, as does His sight: "He, the Exalted and Most Honored, is never lacking in knowing all their affairs." He supports this with two other ayat: "Know they not that Allah knows their secret ideas, and their najwā, and that Allah is the All-Knower of the unseen" (9:78), and "Or do they think that We hear not their secrets and their private najwā? And Our messengers are by them to record" (43:80). That second ayah adds a second layer of exposure — Ibn Kathir notes that Allah's angels record everything such people say, *even though* He already has better knowledge of it and hears them perfectly.

**Why three and five?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers a suggestion: verse 7 specifies the odd numbers three and five probably because Allah prefers that an assembly should comprise an odd number of members. Presented as a probability, not a ruling — and worth noting as the kind of quiet preference the Qurʼān can embed in its choice of examples.

**A beautiful observation on the structure.** Imam Ahmad remarked: "Allah began the Ayah (58:7) by mentioning His knowledge and ended it by mentioning His knowledge." The ayah opens with *Allah knows whatever is in the heavens and the earth* and closes with *Allah is the All-Knower of everything* — the najwā of the plotters is sealed inside His knowledge on both sides, with nowhere to leak out.

And the ayah does not leave that knowledge in the present tense. Before it closes, it names an appointment: "And afterwards on the Day of Resurrection He will inform them of what they did." The record the angels keep is not for Allah's benefit — He has better knowledge of it already. It is for the day it will be read back. Every whispered meeting has a scheduled reading.

## Ayah 8: the ones who went back to it

The word Allah uses is **thumma yaʿūdūna** — "then they *return* to what they were forbidden." The offence is not ignorance; they had been told, and they went back. Ibn Kathir describes them speaking "with persistence and recommending each other to follow their way."

Ayah 8 breaks their whispering into three categories, and Ibn Kathir distinguishes the first two with precision:

- **al-ithm (sin)** — that "which involves themselves." Wrongdoing whose damage falls on the one committing it.
- **al-ʿudwān (wrongdoing / aggression)** — that "which affects others." Sin aimed outward, at somebody else.
- **maʿṣiyat al-Rasūl (disobedience to the Messenger)** — Ibn Kathir says they would speak about defying the Messenger ﷺ and urge one another to keep to that path.

Between them, the three cover the full range: what you do to yourself, what you do to others, and what you do against the guidance.

## The twisted greeting

Then ayah 8 moves from what they said behind the Prophet's ﷺ back to what they said to his face: "when they come to you, they greet you with a greeting wherewith Allah greets you not."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the trick in the words themselves. The proper greeting is **as-salāmu ʿalaykum** — *peace be upon you*. Some of the Jews of Madinah would say **as-sāmu ʿalaykum** — and *as-sām* means **death**. The distortion was a small twist of the tongue, and the difference between the two words was so subtle that the Companions could hardly detect it. They were being cursed in a room full of people, and it sounded like a greeting.

Ibn Kathir records the moment it was caught. Ibn Abi Hatim recorded that ʿA'ishah said: some Jews came to the Prophet ﷺ and greeted him with "As-Sām ʿalayka, O Abul-Qasim." She said back to them, "wa ʿalaykum as-sām" — the same death be upon you. The Prophet ﷺ said to her, **"O ʿA'ishah, Allah does not like rudeness and foul speech."** She said, "Didn't you hear them say, 'As-Sām ʿalayka?'" He ﷺ replied, "Didn't you hear me answering them back by saying, *wa ʿalaykum* — and the same upon you?" And then this ayah was sent down. Ibn Kathir notes that the narration collected in the Sahih has ʿA'ishah saying more sharply, "And be upon you the death, disgrace and curse," and that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to her: **"Allah accepts our supplication against them, but not theirs against us."**

Look closely at what the Prophet ﷺ actually did. He did not miss the insult — he answered it, in two words, exactly and no further. His correction of ʿA'ishah was not that she had defended him, but that she had gone past what was needed into harshness. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the lesson out under the heading *Return Good for Evil*: "even in response to the mischievous words of the infidels, the Muslims should always adopt a soft and noble way." And the closing line — that Allah answers the believers' supplication against them and not theirs against the believers — is a quiet reassurance: their curse is going nowhere. Why raise your voice at a weapon that does not fire?

Ibn Kathir also cites Ibn Jarir's report from Anas bin Malik: a Jew passed the Messenger of Allah ﷺ while he sat with his Companions, greeted them, and they greeted him back. The Prophet ﷺ asked, "Do you know what he just said?" They said, "He said as-salām, O Messenger of Allah." He ﷺ said, "Rather, he said *sām ʿalaykum*" — meaning, may you disgrace your religion. He had the man brought back and asked him directly, "Did you say *sām ʿalaykum*?" The man said yes. So the Prophet ﷺ taught the rule: **"When the people of the Book greet you, say: wa ʿalaykum"** — and the same on you too. Ibn Kathir notes that the basis for this hadith of Anas is in the Sahih, as is a similar report from ʿA'ishah.

## "Why doesn't Allah punish us for what we say?"

The ayah then reports what they said *within themselves*. Ibn Kathir unpacks the reasoning: having twisted the greeting into an insult, they told themselves — *if he were really a Prophet, Allah would have punished us for what we said; Allah knows what we conceal; so had Muhammad been a Prophet, the punishment would already have come in this life.* They treated the absence of an immediate lightning bolt as proof.

Allah's reply is one clause: **"Hell will be sufficient for them; they will enter therein. And worst indeed is that destination."** Ibn Kathir: Hell should be sufficient for them in the Hereafter. Delay is not acquittal. Ibn Kathir also cites a report of Imam Ahmad from ʿAbdullah bin ʿAmr, that the Jews used to say "sām ʿalayka" to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and then say among themselves, "Why does Allah not punish us for what we say?" — after which this ayah was revealed; Ibn Kathir notes its chain is Hasan, though al-Bukhari and Muslim did not collect it.

## Ayah 9: the believers get the same word — and a different ending

Now the address turns: **yā ayyuhā alladhīna āmanū**. The Qurʼān does not tell the believers never to speak privately. It tells them what their private speech must be *for*. Ibn Kathir: Allah is teaching His believing servants to avoid the ways of the disbelievers and hypocrites — "do not hold evil secret counsels like the ignorant disbelieving People of the Scripture and their allies among the hypocrites, who imitate their ways."

Then comes the pivot. The very same three items are forbidden — sin, aggression, disobedience to the Messenger — and in their place two are commanded: **al-birr** (righteousness, doing good) and **al-taqwā** (mindfulness of Allah). The structure is not a ban but a redirection: the private conversation is a tool, and Allah is telling you what to build with it.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states the principle plainly: the condemnation of secret conferences in these ayat "is not unreserved or unqualified… **It is the object or motive of a particular conference that determines its nature.**" Muslims may hold private conferences — to promote good and righteous causes. What they may not do, it adds, is hold a secret conference to harm or hurt another Muslim; and that rule applies to how they treat everyone, not only how enemies treated them.

And the ayah seals it with the reason: "have taqwā of Allah, unto Whom you shall be gathered." Ibn Kathir: He will then inform you of all your deeds and statements; He has counted and recorded them and will justly hold you accountable. Ayah 9 ends where ayah 7 ended — at the gathering where everything whispered is read out.

## Ayah 10: naming the real source, and the limit of its power

Ayah 10 makes the diagnosis: **"Secret counsels are only from Shayṭān, in order that he may cause grief to the believers."** Ibn Kathir is careful about which najwā is meant — the secret talks *where the believers feel anxious*. Those who hold such counsels, he says, do so because of the lures of the devil.

Read the stated purpose closely: **li-yaḥzuna** — *so that he may grieve them*. Not to defeat them, not to destroy them — to make them sad, uneasy, suspicious. That is the whole objective. And the ayah immediately amputates it: "**But he cannot harm them in the least, except as Allah permits.**" Ibn Kathir: the devil seeks to bother the believers, even though his plots will not harm them unless Allah wills it. Anxiety was the entire payload, and anxiety is something you can refuse to hand over.

Hence the final instruction: **"And in Allah let the believers put their trust."** The verb the ayah uses here — *fal-yatawakkal* — comes from **tawakkul**, which means entrusting your affair to Allah and resting your reliance on Him rather than on your own calculations of who might be plotting what. Ibn Kathir gives the practical counsel to anyone who is the subject of evil whispering: seek refuge in Allah and put your trust in Him, for none of it will harm you, Allah willing.

## From the Sunnah: don't do it to each other

Having comforted the believer who is whispered *about*, the passage's teaching turns to the believer who whispers. Ibn Kathir: "The Sunnah also forbids the najwā so that no Muslim is bothered by it."

Imam Ahmad recorded that ʿAbdullah bin Masʿūd said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: **"If you were three, then two of you should not hold a secret counsel in the presence of the third person, because that would cause him to be worried."** Ibn Kathir notes this hadith is collected in the Two Sahihs through a chain containing al-Aʿmash. ʿAbdur-Razzaq narrated from ʿAbdullah bin ʿUmar the same prohibition with an added clause — **"except with his permission"** — and Ibn Kathir notes that Muslim collected this hadith. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites a narration of ʿAbdullah Ibn ʿAbbas recorded in Bukhari, Muslim and other authentic collections to the same effect, and explains the reason: the excluded person "will feel estranged or alienated and possibly suspicions may arise that the two are plotting something against him."

That is the passage coming full circle. The Companion who changed his walking route because two men lowered their voices as he passed — the Sunnah forbids a Muslim from ever making another person feel that.

## Living it

- **Assume the fourth seat is taken.** Ayah 7 is not a warning to be afraid of surveillance; it is an invitation to speak privately the way you would speak publicly. The gap between the two is the exact measure of a problem.
- **Ask what the meeting is *for*.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's rule is the practical test: the motive determines the nature. Private planning for *birr* and *taqwā* is not merely permitted, it is commanded in ayah 9.
- **Never leave the third person out.** In a group of three, do not drop into a private exchange the third cannot share — not without their permission — because of what it does to them.
- **When you are the one being whispered about,** ayah 10 gives you both the diagnosis and the cure: the aim is your grief, the harm is not in their hands, and your response is *tawakkul* — handing the matter over to Allah and relying on Him.
- **Answer insult with exactness, not escalation.** The Prophet ﷺ replied with two words and told ʿA'ishah that Allah does not like rudeness and foul speech — while assuring her that Allah answers the believers' prayer, not theirs.

passages.title: Making room, and the charity before consulting the Prophet
passages.tafsir:
**In one breath:** these three ayat teach the manners of being in the Prophet's ﷺ company — how to behave in the crowded public gathering (ayah 11), and how to behave when you want him to yourself in a private word (ayat 12–13). One passage, two doors into the same room.

What holds them together is a single concern: the Prophet ﷺ was a shared blessing, and a shared blessing has to be handled with courtesy. In ayah 11 the crowding is physical — a full gathering, latecomers left standing. In ayat 12–13 the crowding is on his time and attention — people wanting private consultations, one after another. In both cases Allah does not simply scold; He legislates a small, concrete act — make room; give a charity first — and then reveals how much lies behind that small act. And both halves close by naming the same attribute of Allah: **Khabīr** — rendered at the end of ayah 11 as "And Allah is Well-Acquainted with what you do," and at the end of ayah 13 as "And Allah is All-Aware of what you do." Whether you shift along to make space, or hold back from crowding the Prophet ﷺ, Allah knows exactly what you did and why.

## The scene behind ayah 11

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records the occasion. The Prophet ﷺ was sitting in the **ṣuffah** of the mosque, and the congregation had filled it completely. Then some of the participants of the battle of **Badr** arrived late. They could not find a place to sit, and remained standing.

Picture it: men who had been at Badr, now standing at the back of a full room because nobody wanted to give up a hard-won place close to the Prophet ﷺ. As a mark of respect for them, he ﷺ gave a general order to the entire congregation to spread out and make room for their fellow-believers, and he prayed to Allah to make room for those who did so. Maʿārif adds, gently, that some of them might have complied and there was no problem with them; probably others did not — and so he ﷺ might have told them to rise up and leave. That is the setting of the two commands in the ayah.

Qatādah gives the same picture from a slightly different angle: this ayah was revealed about gatherings in places where Allah is being remembered. When someone would come to join the assemblies of the Messenger ﷺ, those already seated would hesitate to offer them space, so as not to lose their own places. Allah commanded them to spread out and make room for each other.

So the ayah is not about seating charts. It is about a small, very human meanness that shows up precisely where people are gathered for good — the instinct to guard your place near the light.

## "Make room, and Allah will make room for you"

Ibn Kathir draws the principle out plainly: **the reward or recompense depends on the type of action.** You are repaid in the currency you spent. He supports this with two teachings of the Prophet ﷺ — that whoever builds a masjid for Allah, Allah builds for him a house in Paradise; and that whoever relieves a difficulty for a person living in straitened circumstances, Allah will relieve for him the difficulties of this life and the Hereafter, and that Allah helps the servant as long as the servant helps his brother. (Ibn Kathir gives these without naming a collection, and notes there are many similar hadiths.) The shape of the deed becomes the shape of the reward. Make a little room for a man beside you, and Allah widens things for you — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says that if this is done, Allah promises He will widen their scope in the Hereafter, though it is not inconceivable that this room might be created for them in the life of this world as well.

## Who may ask, and who may not

There is a point of wording in ayah 11 that the scholars build a whole etiquette on. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the verse uses the **passive voice** — "when *it is said* to you" — without mentioning who says it or who should say it. So who is entitled to say it?

The answer is settled by the Sunnah. On the authority of ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: **"One of you should not move some other person up from his place and sit in it, but instead, spread out and make room."** Ibn Kathir notes that Imam Ahmad and Imam ash-Shāfiʿī recorded it and that the hadith is recorded in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs; Maʿārif cites it as recorded in the Ṣaḥīḥain and in the Musnad of Ahmad. Ibn Kathir also records from Abū Hurayrah, through Imam Ahmad: "A man should not remove another man from his place and then sit in it. Rather spread out and make room, and Allah will make room for you." Imam Ahmad records it too with the wording, "A man should not leave his place for another man, but rather spread out and make room, and Allah will make room for you."

So the latecomer has no right to say it. He cannot move anyone out, and he cannot force his way into a gathering. Therefore, Maʿārif reasons, the rule would apply to the master of ceremonies, the organisers of the assembly, or the host — and when he asks for a legitimate reason, the guests should comply and avoid a clash with the host. Maʿārif lists reasons this can arise: the host may himself need privacy for his own reason; he may need privacy to share confidential information with special guests; or the capacity of the room cannot accommodate the latecomers and no alternative arrangement can be made, so he may courteously request some of the familiar guests to leave — provided it is certain they will not suffer any loss and will be able to benefit in another session, and provided the host ensures they are not made to feel belittled or hurt in the process.

**The rules Maʿārif draws from the ayah and its traditions:**
1. The members of a gathering must spread out and make space for the latecomers.
2. Latecomers should not remove others and make room for themselves.
3. At times of need, the host or master of ceremonies may courteously request some of those present to leave.
4. Latecomers may not force their way into a congested congregation, but take a position at one side or in a corner. Maʿārif cites Bukhari: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was once sitting in the mosque with the people around him when three persons arrived; one of them could not find space in the congregation, found some space on one side or in a corner, and sat there — and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ praised him highly.

**A further etiquette.** If two people are sitting closely together, a newcomer should not intrude between them. The Prophet ﷺ said: "It is not permissible for any man to break up the meeting of two persons who are sitting together, unless they themselves permit him." (Maʿārif notes that Ibn Kathir cited this tradition and said that Abū Dāwūd and Tirmidhī transmitted it on the authority of Usāmah ibn Laythī.) The reasoning, Maʿārif explains, is that sometimes two people sit together for a specific purpose, and breaking them up might defeat that purpose.

## "And when you are told to rise up"

On **unshuzū** — "rise up" — the sources preserve more than one reading, and it is worth attributing them rather than flattening them. Ibn Kathir reports that it has been said from Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and others that the instruction refers to **war assemblies**: "make room" in those assemblies, and "rise up" meaning *get up to fight*. Qatādah gave it a broader sense: "When you are called to any type of good, then respond."

Both readings share a spirit. The believer is someone who moves when he is called — whether the call is to shift along, to stand and go, or to march.

## The promise that changes everything

Then comes the line that lifts the whole subject: **"Allah will exalt in degrees those of you who believe, and those who have been granted knowledge."**

Ibn Kathir ties it directly back to the etiquette, and this is the heart of it. Do not think, he says, that if one of you makes room for his brother, or rises up when he is commanded to do so, this will diminish his right or his honour. Rather, it *increases* his virtue and status with Allah, and Allah will never let his good deed be lost; He will reward him for it in this life and the Hereafter. **Surely, he who humbles himself by and before the command of his Lord, Allah will elevate his status and make him known by his good behaviour.** And the close of the ayah — "And Allah is Well-Acquainted with what you do" — means, Ibn Kathir says, that Allah is aware of those who deserve this reward and those who are not worthy of it.

Notice that the raising is tied to two things: **faith**, and **being granted knowledge**. Ibn Kathir illustrates this with an incident recorded by Imam Ahmad, reported by Abū al-Ṭufayl ʿĀmir ibn Wāthilah. Nāfiʿ ibn ʿAbd al-Ḥārith met ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb in the area of ʿUsfān. ʿUmar asked whom he had appointed as his deputy for the people of the valley — that is, of Makkah. The answer came: "I appointed Ibn Abzā, one of our freed slaves, as my deputy." ʿUmar said, "You made a freed slave their governor in your absence?" He replied, "O Leader of the Faithful! He has memorised Allah's Book and has knowledge of the regulations of inheritance, along with being a proficient judge." ʿUmar said: "Surely, your Prophet ﷺ has said, **'Verily, Allah elevates some people and degrades others, on account of this Book.'**" Muslim collected this hadith.

That is the ayah walking around in daylight: a freed slave left in charge of Makkah because of what he carried of the Book — and ʿUmar accepting it on the spot.

## Ayat 12–13: the charity before a private word

The subject shifts from the public gathering to the private audience, but the concern is the same — courtesy towards the Prophet ﷺ and towards everyone else who has a claim on him.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the scene. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was preoccupied day and night with educating the people and improving their quality of life. In his general assemblies, all present benefited from his teachings. But there were people who wanted private meetings, and he would grant them — and obviously it was not possible to grant everyone's request, as it required time and effort, and that was difficult. The hypocrites made matters worse: they asked for private audiences in order to hurt the sincere Muslims, and they held protracted conferences with him. Some of the unlettered Muslims also held private audiences longer than was normal or necessary. This made things difficult for him ﷺ.

So Allah provided a way to stop that irksome behaviour and lighten the burden on His Prophet ﷺ. In ayah 12 the believers are told: when you wish to consult the Messenger privately, **spend something in charity beforehand.** Ibn Kathir explains the purpose — the charity cleanses and purifies the one giving it and makes him worthy of having a private counsel with the Prophet ﷺ. Hence the Qur'an's own comment: **"That will be better and purer for you."**

Note the mercy built into the command itself: **"But if you find not [the means for it], then verily, Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful."** Ibn Kathir: "But if you find not" means if he is unable to do so due to poverty; Allah only commanded those who are financially able to give this type of charity. Even the strictest-sounding ruling in this passage arrives with an exemption for the poor already attached.

**Maʿārif adds a detail:** the amount or measure of the charity is not specified in the Qur'an. It was a freewill charity, left to the giver.

## The one man who acted on it

Here the sources converge on a remarkable point. Maʿārif records that when this verse was revealed, ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib was the first Companion to act upon it: he offered **one dinar** in charity and requested a private audience with the Prophet ﷺ. Maʿārif calls it a remarkable coincidence that most of the blessed Companions, because of financial constraints, were unable to act upon this verse before its provision was repealed.

ʿAbd ar-Razzāq recorded that Mujāhid said that ʿAlī said: "No one except me implemented this ayah, until it was abrogated" — and he was reported to have said that it remained in effect for merely an hour. Maʿārif reports that ʿAlī used to say there is a verse in the Qur'an that none before him and none after him has ever acted upon: "none before me" is obvious, and "none after me" means none after him will practise it, because the verse is abrogated.

Ibn Kathir records why. Through ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah from Ibn ʿAbbās: the Muslims kept asking Allah's Messenger ﷺ questions until it became difficult on him. Allah wanted to lighten the burden from His Prophet ﷺ. So when He revealed this, many Muslims were afraid to pay this charity and stopped asking — and afterwards Allah sent down ayah 13, and thus made things easy and lenient for them. Saʿīd ibn Abī ʿArūbah reported from Qatādah and Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān in the same vein: people kept questioning him until they made things difficult for him; then one of them would need to speak to the Prophet ﷺ about a real matter but could not do so until he gave in charity; this became hard on people, and Allah sent down relief from the requirement afterwards. ʿIkrimah and al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī state plainly that the command of ayah 12 was abrogated by the next ayah. Maʿmar reported from Qatādah that the ayah was abrogated after being in effect for only one hour of a day.

## "Were you afraid?"

Ayah 13 opens with a question worth hearing carefully: **"Are you afraid of spending in charity before your private consultation?"**

Ibn Kathir gives the sense: are you afraid that the order to give charity before speaking privately to the Prophet ﷺ remains in effect forever? The question is not a rebuke that closes the door; it is the doorway to relief. Immediately Allah says: **"If then you do it not, and Allah has forgiven you, then perform Ṣalāh and give Zakāh and obey Allah and His Messenger."** Ibn Kathir concludes: therefore Allah abrogated the obligation of giving this charity.

And look at what replaces it. Not nothing — the permanent obligations: **ṣalāh, zakāh, obedience to Allah and His Messenger.** A temporary command is lifted; the lifelong duties are restated in its place. Then the ayah closes by naming Allah as it did in ayah 11: **"And Allah is All-Aware of what you do."**

## Why a ruling that lasted an hour is in the Qur'an

Maʿārif answers this beautifully: **although the ordinance is repealed, it achieved its basic purpose.** The Muslims, because of the dictates of their sincere love, avoided protracted audiences with the Prophet ﷺ so that he would not be inconvenienced in any way. The hypocrites avoided protracted audiences with him because they feared they would be recognised for what they were and their hypocrisy exposed. One ayah, in force for perhaps an hour, achieved all of that without a single person being named or shamed. "Allah knows best!" — as Maʿārif ends.

## Living it

- **Make room.** The passage begins with the most ordinary act imaginable and attaches to it a promise from Allah. Spread out in the row, in the study circle, in the queue — and the One who repays according to the type of the deed will make room for you.
- **Never take someone's place.** Arriving late gives you no claim. Sit at the side. The man in the hadith recorded by Bukhari who quietly took a corner was praised highly by the Prophet ﷺ himself.
- **Do not intrude between two people** who are sitting together, unless they permit you.
- **When the host asks, get up gracefully.** And if you are the host, ask courteously, for a legitimate reason, and never in a way that leaves someone feeling belittled or hurt.
- **Yielding is not losing.** Ibn Kathir's principle governs the whole passage: he who humbles himself before the command of his Lord, Allah elevates his status.
- **Be careful with other people's time**, especially the time of those who serve many. That is the practical residue of ayat 12–13 for us: the private audience is gone, but the manners around a shared, over-stretched blessing remain.
- **Knowledge and faith are what actually lift a person** — not seniority, not proximity to the front row, not lineage. A freed slave was left in charge of Makkah because he carried the Book.

passages.title: The hypocrites who allied with Allah's enemies
passages.tafsir:
These six ayat describe a group of hypocrites and the false oaths they used. Ibn Kathir sums up the charge: Allah chastises them for secretly aiding and supporting the disbelievers, even though in reality they were neither with the disbelievers nor with the Muslims. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān frames it the same way — Allah condemns the hypocrites who had secretly formed an alliance with a people who challenge Allah and His Messenger ﷺ, while in effect belonging neither to the Muslims nor to them. Running through the passage is the oath they swore to cover the gap: sworn falsely and knowingly (ayah 14), used as a screen (ayah 16), and sworn again before Allah on the Day of Resurrection (ayah 18).

## "Have you not seen…"

Ayah 14 opens: **alam tara** — "Have you not seen those who take as friends a people upon whom is the wrath of Allah?"

Ibn Kathir explains that the people referred to here are the Jews, with whom the hypocrites were allies in secret. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes the same secret alliance, with a people who challenge Allah and His Messenger ﷺ, and notes that in effect the hypocrites belonged neither to the Muslims nor to them. Consequently, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds, Allah has prepared for them a humiliating and condign chastisement.

To capture that in-between state, Ibn Kathir brings a verse from elsewhere in the Qur'an describing the hypocrites as **mudhabdhabīn** — "swaying between this and that, belonging neither to these nor to those; and he whom Allah sends astray, you will not find for him a way" (4:143). The image is of swaying between two sides and belonging to neither. That is exactly what ayah 14 says of them: **mā hum minkum wa lā minhum** — "they are neither of you nor of them." Ibn Kathir's gloss is precise: these hypocrites are neither with the believers, nor with their allies the Jews.

## The lie they knew was a lie

The last phrase of ayah 14 is exact: they swear to a lie **wa hum yaʿlamūn** — "while they know." Ibn Kathir explains that the hypocrites lie when they vow, knowing that they are lying — which, he notes, is called the vow of Al-Ghamus. He adds, "We seek refuge with Allah from their ways."

Then he draws out something subtle. When these men met the believers they said that they believed, and when they went to the Messenger ﷺ they swore to him by Allah that they were believers. Ibn Kathir observes that their statement — that Muhammad ﷺ is Allah's Prophet — is true in essence. Their lie lay elsewhere: they knew they were lying in their vow, and they knew that they had not declared their true creed. This is why Allah testifies here that they lie in their vows and know that they are lying. A statement true in itself is still a lie on the tongue of someone who does not hold it in his heart. That is why the passage fixes on the heart rather than on the formula.

## The occasion: two men and an oath

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records, citing Qurtubi, that according to some reports the words "and they swear false oaths" were revealed in connection with ʿAbdullah ibn Ubayy and ʿAbdullah ibn Nabtal. One day the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was sitting with his noble Companions and said to them: "Soon a person will come to you whose heart will be the heart of a tyrant and who sees through the Shaitan's eyes." Soon afterwards ʿAbdullah ibn Nabtal, the hypocrite, entered — blue-eyed, wheat-coloured, short-statured and skimpy-bearded. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ asked him why he and his comrades used obscene words against him. He swore that he had not done so. He then called his comrades, and they too took this false oath. Allah told the Prophet ﷺ about their lie and their profane oath.

## The oath as a screen — ayah 16

Ayah 16 gives the mechanism: **ittakhadhū aymānahum junnah** — "they have made their oaths a screen." Ibn Kathir explains that the hypocrites pretended to be believers and concealed disbelief under the shield of their false oaths. Many people were unaware of their true stance and were thus deceived by those oaths.

The consequence follows in the same ayah: **fa-ṣaddū ʿan sabīl Allāh** — "thus they hinder others from the path of Allah." Because their oaths were believed, Ibn Kathir says, some people were hindered from the path of Allah. The harm did not stop with themselves.

The two torments named in this stretch are distinct. Ayah 15 promises **ʿadhāban shadīdan**, a severe torment — which Ibn Kathir ties to their evil deeds, their aid and support of the disbelievers, and their deceit and betrayal of the believers. Ayah 16 promises **ʿadhābun muhīn**, a *humiliating* torment — which Ibn Kathir explains as the recompense for belittling the significance of swearing by the Mighty Name of Allah while lying and concealing betrayal.

## What will not help them — ayah 17

Ayah 17 names two things and says neither will avail them: **amwāluhum wa awlāduhum** — their wealth and their children. Ibn Kathir's comment is stark: none of their possessions can avert the affliction when it is sent their way. Then the ayah states their end — they will be the dwellers of the Fire, to dwell therein forever.

## Swearing on the Day of Resurrection — ayah 18

Ayah 18 turns to the Day when Allah resurrects them all together — which Ibn Kathir explains as the Day of Resurrection, when He will gather them all together and leave none of them out. There, "they will swear to Him as they swear to you." Ibn Kathir explains: they will swear to Allah the Exalted and Most Honored that they were following the guidance and the correct path, just as they used to swear to the believers in this worldly life.

Ibn Kathir then gives the reason the habit outlives them: those who live following a certain path will most likely die while on it, and thus they will be resurrected upon their path.

Then: **wa yaḥsabūna annahum ʿalā shayʼ** — "and they think that they have something." Ibn Kathir explains that the hypocrites will think their vows will help them with Allah just as those vows helped with people, who were obliged to treat them as they pretended to be — Muslim. Allah rebukes this idea of theirs at once: **alā innahum humu-l-kādhibūn** — "verily, they are liars!" Ibn Kathir notes the wording stresses that they are lying.

## Whose party they really joined — ayah 19

Ayah 19 closes the passage: **istaḥwadha ʿalayhimu-sh-shayṭān** — "the Shaytan has overpowered them. So he has made them forget the remembrance of Allah." Ibn Kathir explains that Shaytan has taken over their hearts to the point that he made them forget Allah the Exalted and Most Honored — and this, he says, is what the devil does to those whom he controls.

**From the Sunnah.** At this point Ibn Kathir cites a hadith recorded by Abu Dawud, in which Abu Ad-Darda' said that he heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: "Any three in a village or desert among whom the Salah is not called for, will have the Shaytan control them. Therefore, adhere to the Jamaʿah, for the wolf eats from the strayed sheep." Ibn Kathir notes the addition of Zaʼidah, that As-Saʼib said Jamaʿah here refers to praying in congregation.

The hadith carries the very expression the ayah uses — *istaḥwadha ʿalayhim ash-shayṭān*, "the Shaytan has overpowered them" — which is why Ibn Kathir places it here. Where the ayah states the condition, the hadith gives the practical direction: keep to the congregation.

The ayah then gives the label: **ulāʼika ḥizbu-sh-shayṭān** — "they are the party of Shaytan," which Ibn Kathir applies to those who are controlled by the devil and, as a result, forgot the remembrance of Allah. And the verdict: "Verily, it is the party of Shaytan that will be the losers!"

## Living it: the line the scholars draw

Ayah 14 raises a question every Muslim living among non-Muslims will ask, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān addresses it directly.

**What is forbidden.** It is not permissible to have a friendly intimacy with the enemies of Allah and His Messenger ﷺ — and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is explicit that this is not about one community: it applies whether the unbelievers are Jews, or Christians, or pagans, or of any other creed. The term for it is **muwālāh**, "intimate friendship": love, affection and intimacy coming from the heart, involving intense emotional commitment, which necessarily includes having love for the other's way of life. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān argues that even rationally this is not possible — the capital asset of a believer is the love of Allah, while a non-believer relishes opposing and challenging Him, and it is not possible for a person to have sincere love for someone and at the same time be intimate with that person's enemy. This kind of friendship, it says, is limited to sincere Muslims; the Qur'an on many occasions strictly prohibits Muslims from having this sort of relationship with non-Muslims, and any Muslim who does will be seen to fall in the circle of unbelievers.

**What is permitted.** Set against that, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes a different category: the relationship based on sympathy, kindness and concern. It includes charitable assistance and support; business, commercial and trade dealings and economic cooperation; condolence and consolation; and any well-meaning attitude of well-being and welfare. Barring unbelievers who are at war with the believers, this kind of relationship is permissible with all other non-Muslims — and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points to the paradigm of the Holy Prophet ﷺ and the noble Companions as ample testimony to this practice. For the fuller treatment it refers the reader to its own commentary on Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 3:28–30, where it distinguishes **muwālāt** (intimate friendship), **muwāsāt** (sympathy), **muʿāmalāt** (dealings) and **mudārāh** (cordiality).

**The conditions.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān attaches three: such a relationship must not be harmful to the cause of religion; it must not create laxity in one's faith and practice of Islam; and it must not harm, hurt or injure other Muslims.

So the passage is not asking a believer to be cold, ungenerous or suspicious towards his neighbours — the sources go out of their way to protect kindness and good dealing. What it condemns is what the hypocrites in ayah 14 actually did: a secret alliance with those who challenge Allah and His Messenger ﷺ, covered over with oaths sworn in Allah's name.

**And the mirror to hold up.** These were men who came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and swore by Allah that they were believers, while knowing they had not declared their true creed. The warning is about that mechanism: a tongue that says what the heart does not hold, and Allah's own Name used to cover it. And the remedy the sources place at the end of this passage is small and concrete — adhere to the Jamaʿah, praying in congregation, for the wolf eats from the strayed sheep.

passages.title: Allah's party and His decreed victory
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat close Surah al-Mujadilah by dividing humanity into two camps and announcing, in advance, which one wins. Ayah 20 names the losers, ayah 21 states Allah's written decree of victory, and ayah 22 describes the people on the winning side — not by their numbers or weapons, but by where their hearts have placed their loyalty. What holds the passage together is a single question: when love of Allah and love of your own flesh and blood pull in opposite directions, which one gives way?

## The line in the ground (ayah 20)

Ayah 20 speaks of *alladhīna yuḥāddūna Allāha wa rasūlah* — those who "defy" or "oppose" Allah and His Messenger ﷺ. Ibn Kathir describes them as the rebellious and stubborn disbelievers who defy Allah and His Messenger ﷺ, those who do not embrace the religion and stay away from Truth, and he gives the image that they "are in one area, while the guidance is in another area." Two separate places, not one shared ground.

The verdict on them is *fī al-adhallīn* — "they will be among those most humiliated." Ibn Kathir explains that they are "among the miserable, the cast out, banished from goodness; they are the humiliated ones in this life and the Hereafter." Note the two timeframes he insists on: this humiliation is not merely a sentence deferred to the Day of Judgement, and it is not merely a worldly setback either. It reaches across both.

## "Allah has decreed" (ayah 21)

Ayah 21 is the hinge of the passage: *kataba Allāhu la-aghlibanna anā wa rusulī* — "Allah has decreed: 'Verily, I and My Messengers shall be the victorious.'" The verb *kataba* means to write, and Ibn Kathir takes it in its fullest sense: Allah "has decreed, written in the First Book, and decided in the decree that He has willed — which can never be resisted, changed or prevented — that final victory is for Him, His Book, His Messengers and the faithful believers, in this life and the Hereafter."

Notice who is gathered into that sentence. Ibn Kathir does not stop at Allah's own victory: the decree covers Him, His Book, His Messengers, and the faithful believers together. The messengers' triumph is not a separate matter that might or might not accompany His. It is written in the same decree.

Ibn Kathir sets this alongside two other verses that say the same thing: *"Surely, the (good) end is for those who have Taqwa"* (11:49), and *"Verily, We will indeed make victorious Our Messengers and those who believe in the life of this world and on the Day when the witnesses will stand forth"* (40:51–52). The pattern is consistent across the Qur'an — an outcome already settled, whatever a given generation happens to see.

The ayah then seals the promise with two of Allah's names: *Qawiyy*, the All-Powerful, and *ʿAzīz*, the Almighty. These are the guarantee that the decree will hold. As Ibn Kathir puts it, "the Almighty, All-Powerful has decreed that He shall prevail over His enemies. Indeed, this is the final judgement and a matter ordained; the final triumph and victory are for the believers in this life and the Hereafter."

## The people of the promise (ayah 22)

Having settled the outcome, ayah 22 turns to the people who belong to the winning side: *lā tajidu qawman* — "You will not find any people who believe in Allah and the Last Day, making friendship with those who oppose Allah and His Messenger, even though they were their fathers or their sons or their brothers or their kindred." Ibn Kathir reads the practical instruction inside it: "do not befriend the deniers, even if they are among the closest relatives."

And the ayah names the relatives one by one, leaving no exemption: *fathers, sons, brothers, kindred*. Ibn Kathir places beside it *"Let not the believers take the disbelievers as friends instead of the believers... except if you indeed fear a danger from them"* (3:28) — a verse that contains its own allowance for the believer under genuine threat — and *"Say: If your fathers, your sons, your brothers, your wives, your kindred, the wealth that you have gained, the commerce in which you fear a decline, and the dwellings in which you delight are dearer to you than Allah and His Messenger... then wait until Allah brings about His decision"* (9:24).

## Why these four relations? Reports from Badr

Classical commentary reads the four categories against real faces. Ibn Kathir reports from Saʿid bin ʿAbdul-ʿAziz and others that the ayah was revealed in the case of **Abu ʿUbaydah ʿAmir bin ʿAbdullah bin al-Jarrah**, who killed his disbelieving father during the battle of Badr — and adds the striking sequel that when ʿUmar bin al-Khattab placed the matter of the Khilafah in the consultation of six men after him, he said, "If Abu ʿUbaydah were alive, I would have appointed him the Khalifah."

It was also said, Ibn Kathir continues, that each phrase answers to a particular Companion at Badr: *"their fathers"* to Abu ʿUbaydah; *"their sons"* to Abu Bakr as-Siddiq, when he intended to kill his son ʿAbdur-Rahman, then still a disbeliever; *"their brothers"* to Musʿab bin ʿUmayr, who killed his brother ʿUbayd bin ʿUmayr; *"their kindred"* to ʿUmar, who killed one of his relatives that day; and it was also said that the ayah was revealed in the case of Hamzah, ʿAli and ʿUbaydah bin al-Harith, who killed their close relatives ʿUtbah, Shaybah and al-Walid bin ʿUtbah that day. Ibn Kathir closes the whole list with **"Allah knows best"** — and the reports themselves are introduced with "it was also said," which is how the scholars mark a transmitted opinion rather than a settled certainty.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Qurtubi, gathers a set of incidents with the same lesson, some of them differing in detail from Ibn Kathir's. It relates that **ʿAbdullah, son of ʿAbdullah bin Ubayy** — the son of the leader of the hypocrites in Madinah — heard his father make blasphemous remarks against the Prophet ﷺ and came to seek permission to kill him, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ stopped him. It relates that **Abu Bakr** heard his father Abu Quhafah utter insulting words against the Prophet ﷺ and struck him so hard that he fell down, and when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ heard about it he advised Abu Bakr not to do it again. And it places Abu ʿUbaydah's killing of his father **at Uhud** rather than Badr, describing how his father came face to face with him time and again on the battlefield while Abu ʿUbaydah kept moving out of the way as a mark of respect, until his father's persistence left him no choice. Where the reports differ over which battle, the sound course is to note the difference rather than to force one account.

Two things stand out in this material. First, in the two cases just mentioned it is Allah's Messenger ﷺ himself who restrained his Companions — the son was stopped, and Abu Bakr was advised not to repeat it. Second, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states the principle plainly: **the bond of belief transcends all other bonds, even the close ties of blood** — adding that this description fits all the noble Companions, and that this set of verses was revealed to laud them.

Ibn Kathir mentions one more scene in the same spirit: the Prophet's ﷺ consultation with his Companions over the captives of Badr. Abu Bakr thought they should accept ransom so the Muslims could strengthen themselves, noting that the captives were cousins and kindred who might yet embrace Islam by Allah's help. ʿUmar took the opposite view: "Let me kill so-and-so, my relative, and let ʿAli kill ʿAqil... Let us make it known to Allah that we have no mercy in our hearts for the idolators."

## What kind of "friendship" is forbidden

This is the point where careful readers most often go wrong, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is precise about it. The forbidden thing is **muwālāt** — intimate friendship: love, affection and intimacy "coming from the heart involving intense emotional commitment," which necessarily includes loving the other's way of life. That bond, the commentary says, is limited to sincere Muslims, and it is not permissible to have a friendly intimacy with the enemies of Allah and His Messenger ﷺ — "whether the unbelievers are Jews, or Christians, or pagans or of any other creed." The commentary adds a rational argument: the capital asset of a believer is the love of Allah, while a non-believer relishes in opposing and challenging Him; it is not possible for a person to have sincere love for someone and at the same time to have intimacy with that person's enemy.

Distinct from this, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān identifies relationships built on **sympathy, kindness and concern** — charitable assistance and support, business, commercial and trade dealings, economic cooperation, condolence and consolation, and any well-meaning attitude of well-being and welfare. Barring unbelievers who are at war with the believers, this kind of relationship is **permissible with all other non-Muslims**, and the paradigm of the Holy Prophet ﷺ and the noble Companions in this direction is ample testimony to it. The commentary sets conditions: such a relationship must not be harmful to the cause of religion, must not create laxity in one's faith and practice of Islam, and must not harm, hurt or injure other Muslims. For the full treatment of *muwālāt* (intimate friendship), *muwāsāt* (sympathy), *muʿāmalāt* (dealings) and *mudārāh* (cordiality), it refers the reader to its own commentary on Al ʿImran 3:28–30.

**A ruling extended.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that many jurists have ruled that this applies equally to Muslims who transgress or violate the sacred laws of the Shariah, or who in practice turn away from them: sincere Muslims should not maintain intimate friendship with such transgressors, because intimacy with them is possible only if the germs of transgression are already lurking in the one befriending them. Sympathy, dealings and cordiality with them are a different matter, to the degree of necessity. In this connection the commentary, citing Qurtubi, records that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to pray, *"O Allah, do not give any transgressor the upper hand over me."* The explanation offered is subtle and worth sitting with: whoever has the upper hand is most likely to get his own way — he shows kindness to people, and noble persons, on account of that kindness, feel obliged to return it with love. And so the heart is quietly bought.

## What Allah puts into such hearts

Ayah 22 does not leave these believers to their own strength. *Ulāʾika kataba fī qulūbihim al-īmān* — "For such He has written faith in their hearts." The same verb *kataba* that decreed victory in ayah 21 now writes faith into the heart: the outcome outside and the conviction inside are both His writing. Ibn Kathir says that those who have the quality of not befriending those who oppose Allah and His Messenger ﷺ, even if they are their fathers or brothers, are the ones in whose hearts Allah has decreed faith — "meaning, happiness — and made faith dear to their hearts and happiness reside therein." As-Suddi's plain reading is: "He has placed faith in their hearts."

Then: *wa ayyadahum bi-rūḥin minhu* — "and strengthened them with Ruh from Himself." Ibn ʿAbbas explained this simply as "He gave them strengths." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Qurtubi, reports two views among the authorities of tafsir: some hold that *rūḥ* here stands for a light which radiates from Allah and enters the heart of the believer, urging him to perform righteous deeds and becoming the source of the heart's peace and contentment — and that this tranquility and satisfaction is itself the source of great strength and power; others hold that it stands for the Holy Qur'an and its arguments, which are the believer's real strength and power. Both readings say the same essential thing: the firmness these people showed was not raw human resolve. It was supplied.

## The exchange of pleasure

The reward follows: Gardens beneath which rivers flow, dwelling there forever, *raḍiya Allāhu ʿanhum wa raḍū ʿanh* — "Allah is well pleased with them, and they are well pleased with Him."

Ibn Kathir finds "a beautiful secret" in that phrase placed just here. When the believers became enraged against their own relatives and kindred in Allah's cause, Allah **compensated them by being pleased with them and making them pleased with Him**, from what He granted them of eternal delight, ultimate victory and encompassing favour. They gave up one *riḍā* and were given a far greater one.

## The party of Allah

The passage ends by naming them: *ulāʾika ḥizbullāh* — "They are the party of Allah." Ibn Kathir explains that this means His servants who are worthy of earning His honour. And then the closing call: "Verily, the party of Allah will be the successful." Ibn Kathir reads this as asserting their success, happiness and triumph in this life and the Hereafter.

Ibn Kathir sets it deliberately against ayah 19, a few lines earlier, which ended: "Verily, the party of Shaytan will be the losers!" Everyone belongs to one party or the other; the two verses answer each other, and with this the surah — and Ibn Kathir's commentary on it — comes to its close.

## Living it

- **Take the promise of ayah 21 as settled fact, not sentiment.** The believer who is losing — argued down, outnumbered, out of step with his age — is being told that the outcome was written in the First Book, and can never be resisted, changed or prevented.
- **Locate the boundary correctly.** What ayah 22 forbids is *muwālāt*, intimate friendship of the heart, with those who oppose Allah and His Messenger ﷺ — not decency toward the non-Muslims around you. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is explicit that kindness, trade, cooperation, condolence and goodwill are permitted, and the practice of the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions is the evidence.
- **Watch what draws your heart.** The lesson drawn from the Prophet's ﷺ prayer against a transgressor gaining the upper hand is that affection is more often bought by kindness and obligation than by argument. Ask honestly who has that leverage over you.
- **Do not confuse zeal with obedience.** The Companion who sought permission to kill his own father was stopped by the Prophet ﷺ; Abu Bakr was advised not to strike his father again. Loyalty to Allah is measured in the heart's allegiance, and its expression is governed by the Messenger's ﷺ instruction, not by our own heat.
- **Expect the exchange.** Whatever affection is genuinely surrendered for Allah's sake is not simply lost. The ayah answers the loss with His pleasure — and, remarkably, with your own contentment in Him.
